cards.front: What should you know about non-renewable energy resource?
cards.back: A resource that will run out one day because it is being used up faster than it can be replaced. Examples: fossil fuels and nuclear fuel.

cards.front: What should you know about renewable energy resource?
cards.back: A resource that will never run out (or can be replaced within a human lifetime). Examples: solar, wind, hydroelectric, tidal, geothermal, biomass, wave.

cards.front: What should you know about fossil fuels?
cards.back: Coal, oil and natural gas — formed from the remains of ancient organisms over millions of years. They are non-renewable and produce carbon dioxide when burned.

cards.front: What should you know about current uk energy mix?
cards.back: The UK generates most of its electricity from natural gas, with a growing proportion from renewables (especially wind and solar). Coal use has dropped significantly. Nuclear provides a steady base load.

cards.front: What should you know about fossil fuels remain dominant because?
cards.back: they are reliable (available on demand), the infrastructure already exists (power stations, gas pipelines, petrol stations), and they are relatively cheap to set up compared to some renewable alternatives.

cards.front: What should you know about we need to transition to renewables because?
cards.back: fossil fuels are finite and will run out, burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ which causes climate change, and pollution from fossil fuels harms health and the environment.

cards.front: Recall a key point about P3 National And Global Energy
cards.back: You need to interpret energy mix data from charts and tables, calculate percentages from given data, and compare costs of different energy sources. Working with percentage change is also important when analysing trends in energy use over time.

cards.front: What should you know about answers?
cards.back: (a) Country A renewables = wind 25% + solar 10% + hydro 5% = 40%. Country B renewables = wind 10% + solar 20% + hydro 10% = 40%. (b) Advantage: replacing coal with wind and nuclear would eliminate CO₂ emissions from coal, reducing the country's contribution to climate change. Disadvantage: nuclear power stations are very expensive and take many years to build, and wind is intermittent so cannot fully replace the reliable base-load that coal provides. (c) The claim is too simplistic. While solar may be cheap to run, Country B already generates 20% from solar — expanding further has limitations
